what_its_for: This device delivers insulin under your skin (subcutaneously) to help control your blood sugar levels. Insulin is used to treat diabetes (Type 1 or Type 2). It helps your body use sugar from the food you eat for energy and keeps your blood sugar from getting too high.
how_to_take: 1. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water before handling the device. 2. Check the insulin — it should look clear (or evenly cloudy for certain types). Do not use it if you see particles, clumps, or discoloration. 3. Choose an injection site — the belly (abdomen), outer thigh, upper arm, or buttocks are common spots. Rotate sites each time to prevent skin problems. 4. Clean the injection site with an alcohol swab and let it dry completely. 5. Pinch a fold of skin gently if you are thin. Insert the needle at the angle your healthcare provider recommended (usually 90 degrees, or 45 degrees if you are very lean). 6. Press the button or plunger slowly and steadily to inject the full dose. 7. Hold the device in place for 5 to 10 seconds after injecting, then remove the needle. 8. Do not rub the injection site after removing the needle. 9. Dispose of the used needle safely in a puncture-resistant sharps container. Never recap or share needles.
dosing: Your doctor will prescribe a specific dose tailored to you. This device is designed to deliver up to 40 units per injection. Your dose may change based on your blood sugar readings, meals, activity level, illness, or stress. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your healthcare provider first. Check your blood sugar as directed to make sure your dose is working correctly.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose of your insulin, what you should do depends on the type of insulin you are using. For long-acting insulin (once-daily basal insulin): Take it as soon as you remember, as long as it is not too close to the time of your next scheduled dose. For rapid-acting or short-acting mealtime insulin: If you forget to take it before a meal and you have already eaten, skip that dose — do not double up. Check your blood sugar and contact your doctor or diabetes care team for guidance. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Keep a log of missed doses to share with your doctor.
storage: Store unopened insulin vials, pens, or cartridges in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze insulin — frozen insulin must be thrown away. Keep insulin away from direct heat and sunlight. Once opened or in use, most insulin can be kept at room temperature (below 77°F / 25°C) for up to 28 to 30 days, depending on the brand — check your specific product label. Store the device with the needle tip pointing up or horizontally to avoid air bubbles. Check the expiration date before every use and throw away expired insulin. Keep insulin and this device out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid injecting insulin into skin that is red, bruised, swollen, scarred, or has hard lumps (lipohypertrophy). Avoid skipping meals after taking mealtime insulin, as this can cause low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Avoid drinking alcohol without eating, as it can cause your blood sugar to drop dangerously low. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if your blood sugar is low or unstable. Avoid exposing insulin to extreme heat or cold (do not leave it in a hot car or near a freezer vent). Avoid sharing your insulin device or needles with anyone else, even family members — this can spread infections. Do not mix different types of insulin unless your doctor has specifically told you to do so.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek medical help right away if you experience: signs of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) such as shakiness, sweating, confusion, dizziness, fast heartbeat, or fainting — especially if it does not improve quickly after eating sugar; signs of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) such as increased thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, or fruity-smelling breath; skin changes at injection sites such as lumps, pitting, or redness that does not go away; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling, trouble breathing, or chest tightness; blood sugar readings that are consistently too high or too low; nausea, vomiting, or illness that is making it hard for you to eat or take your insulin; or if you are unsure whether you took your dose or how much you took.
when_it_works: How quickly insulin starts working depends on the type: Rapid-acting insulin (such as Humalog, NovoLog, Apidra) starts working within 10 to 30 minutes, peaks in 1 to 3 hours, and lasts 3 to 5 hours. Short-acting regular insulin (such as Humulin R, Novolin R) starts working in 30 to 60 minutes, peaks in 2 to 4 hours, and lasts 5 to 8 hours. Long-acting insulin (such as Lantus, Levemir, Tresiba) starts working in 1 to 2 hours, has little to no peak, and lasts up to 24 hours or longer. It may take several days to weeks of consistent use and dose adjustments for your blood sugar to reach your target range. Work closely with your doctor during this time.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Insulin is considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding, but your dose will likely need to change as your body changes. Tell your doctor immediately if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to insulin and at higher risk for low blood sugar. Closer monitoring and possible dose adjustments may be needed. Children and teens: Dosing in children is carefully calculated by weight and age. Parents and caregivers should receive thorough training before using this device. Kidney or liver disease: These conditions can affect how insulin works in your body and may require dose adjustments. Always tell your doctor about all your medical conditions and all medications, vitamins, and supplements you take, as many drugs can raise or lower your blood sugar.
